questions.question: What's driving the request for VLSI notes?
questions.why_it_matters: An exam cheat-sheet highlights formulas and common questions; an interview guide stresses trade-off talking points; a project reference includes tool flows and sign-off checklists; a research map cites recent papers and open problems.

options.label: Exam / course revision
options.implication: condenses each topic to definitions, key equations, and typical numerical problems — ~15 pages

options.label: Job interview prep
options.implication: organises by frequently-asked areas (timing, power, verification, analog basics) with 'why this matters' talking points — ~20 pages

options.label: Active design project
options.implication: adds a runnable RTL-to-GDS flow checklist, common DRC/LVS errors, and sign-off deliverables — ~30 pages

options.label: Research / literature survey

questions.question: Which background best matches you right now?
questions.why_it_matters: A beginner needs MOS physics and stick diagrams explained; a digital-logic student can skip to synthesis and timing; a practicing analog engineer wants digital-back-end flow; a senior designer only needs advanced-nodes and methodology updates.

options.label: No prior semiconductor background
options.implication: starts with energy bands, p-n junction, MOSFET I-V, and stick diagrams — adds ~8 foundational pages

options.label: Digital logic / computer architecture course done
options.implication: skips device physics; opens with CMOS inverter VTC, then combinational / sequential layout — saves ~8 pages

options.label: Analog / RF circuit experience, new to digital back-end
options.implication: assumes small-signal models; focuses on standard-cell flow, STA, power grid, and sign-off — ~22 pages

options.label: 2+ tape-outs, need advanced-node updates
options.implication: jumps straight to FinFET/GAA effects, DTCO, PPA optimisation, and ML-driven flows — ~18 pages

questions.default_label: Digital logic / computer architecture course done

questions.question: What should the notes let you do afterwards?
questions.why_it_matters: Explaining concepts needs clear narratives; reading specs needs vocabulary and spec-breakdown tables; designing a block needs worked RTL-to-layout examples; running full flow needs tool scripts and sign-off checklists.

options.label: Explain VLSI concepts to peers

options.label: Read foundry PDK docs and spec sheets

options.label: Design and verify a small digital block (ALU, FIFO, small CPU)
options.implication: provides coded RTL, synthesis constraints, floorplan, and STA scripts for a 4-bit RISC-V core — ~35 pages

options.label: Execute a full RTL-to-GDS flow with sign-off
options.implication: adds complete flow scripts (DC/ICC/PT/Calibre), UPF power intent, and a tape-out checklist — ~40 pages

ATPG & Fault Coverage
built_from: Design for Testability (Scan, BIST, Boundary Scan)

judgements.why: Foundation for every CMOS circuit topic; exam questions routinely ask about threshold voltage, body effect, channel-length modulation, and I-V characteristics.
Core to understanding why designs work as they do; scaling trends (Dennard, constant-field, constant-voltage) are standard exam material.
Undergraduate VLSI exams always include process flow (oxidation, photolithography, etch, doping, metallization) and cross-section interpretation.
Lambda-based rules, stick diagrams, and DRC/LVS concepts are directly tested — students must draw layouts and check rule compliance.
Standard exam skill: convert a logic function to stick diagram, optimize transistor ordering via Euler path, estimate area.
The canonical building block; VTC, noise margins, delay (tau model, Elmore), and power are exam staples.
NAND, NOR, AOI, OAI sizing for equal rise/fall delay, logical effort introduction — all standard exam content.
Frequently examined for area/delay trade-offs, voltage drop (Vth loss), and specific circuits (mux, XOR).
Precharge/evaluate, charge sharing, clock feedthrough, keeper sizing — common exam questions on high-speed design.
Master-slave, edge-triggered, setup/hold time derivation, metastability — core sequential logic exam material.
Directly tested with waveform analysis; students must compute max clock frequency given path delays.
Clock tree basics, skew vs. jitter, useful skew for timing closure — standard undergraduate topic.
Path-based vs. graph-based, setup/hold checks, slack computation — often a dedicated exam question.
Breakdown of P = αCV²f + I_leak·V + P_sc; exam problems on activity factor, capacitance estimation, leakage components.
Clock gating, power gating, multi-Vt, DVFS, operand isolation — standard coverage in modern curricula.
Elmore delay, Pi/T models, crosstalk noise/glitch, repeater insertion optimization — all exam-relevant.
6T cell stability (SNM), read/write assist, sense amps, row/column decoders — major memory exam topic.
1T1C cell, charge sharing, sense amp operation, refresh — standard memory coverage.
Mask ROM, NOR/NAND flash basics, floating gate — lighter coverage but still appears in exams.
Ripple-carry, carry-lookahead, prefix adders; array/Booth/Wallace multipliers; barrel shifters — classic datapath exam questions.
ALU control, flag logic, multi-port register file bitcell and layout — integrated datapath exam problems.
Stuck-at fault equivalence/collapsing, delay fault models — theoretical foundation for DFT exam questions.

judgements.concept: Design for Testability (Scan, BIST, Boundary Scan)
judgements.why: Scan chain operation, LFSR/MISR for BIST, JTAG (IEEE 1149.1) — standard DFT exam coverage.
D-algorithm, PODEM, fault simulation, coverage metrics — often tested conceptually.
High-level flow understanding (synthesis → floorplan → place → route → signoff) is exam baseline knowledge.
Technology mapping, area/delay trade-offs, retiming, constant propagation — synthesis exam questions are common.
Partitioning, placement algorithms (min-cut, simulated annealing, quadratic), global/detailed routing — methodology exam content.
DRC rule decks, LVS netlist vs. layout, antenna rules — signoff verification is standard curriculum.
Typically graduate-level (SSTA, parametric yield); undergraduate exams mention variation qualitatively but rarely require statistical methods.
Device reliability physics is usually a graduate topic; undergrad courses may name-drop EM/IR drop but not model them.
Advanced technology node content; most undergraduate curricula still teach planar CMOS with FinFET as a 'future/advanced' note.
Emerging packaging/integration topic; not part of standard undergraduate VLSI semester exam scope.
